title: System Logging and Monitoring
markdown:
# System Logging and Monitoring

Every action on a Linux system leaves a trace. When a service starts or stops, when a user authenticates, when the kernel detects a hardware fault, when a daemon encounters an error — all of it gets recorded. These records are called **logs**, and they are the most reliable source of truth you have when something goes wrong.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/Logging.svg)

System logging in Linux is handled by two complementary systems: **systemd-journald**, which captures structured logs from every service and the kernel into a binary journal, and **rsyslog**, which writes human-readable text files under `/var/log/`. Learning to navigate both — and to manage log files before they consume your disk — is a core skill for any Linux administrator.

By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

- Navigate the `/var/log` directory and understand what lives there
- Use `journalctl` to query the systemd journal with powerful filters
- Use `tail -f` to monitor logs in real time
- Use `logger` to write custom messages to syslog
- Filter and analyze log files using `grep`
- Configure log rotation with `logrotate` to manage log file sizes

## The Scenario: AppTrack Is Down

**AppTrack** is a lightweight API server that tracks user activity for a web platform. It runs as a `systemd` service and writes its own application logs to `/var/log/apptrack/apptrack.log`.

Last night, it went silent. No responses, no errors returned to users — just nothing. You need to figure out:

1. When did it go down?
2. What was happening just before it crashed?
3. How do we prevent this from happening again?

To investigate, we will build the environment ourselves. Here is what we will create:

| What | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `/var/log/apptrack/apptrack.log` | A log file showing AppTrack's startup, normal operation, warnings, and final crash |
| System journal entries | Crash messages injected via `logger` to practice `journalctl` filtering |
| `/etc/logrotate.d/apptrack` | A rotation config to keep the log file from growing out of control |

Each piece maps directly to the commands we will learn next.

## Part 1: The Linux Logging Architecture

Before we dive into incident investigation, let's understand where Linux stores its logs and why.

Linux logging works at two levels:

| Layer | What it is | Key location |
|-------|-----------|--------------|
| **Kernel logs** | Messages from the Linux kernel itself | `dmesg`, (or `/var/log/kern.log` if available) |
| **System logs** | Messages from services, daemons, and userspace | `/var/log/syslog`(if rsyslog is configured), `journalctl` |

Modern Linux systems use **systemd-journald** to collect logs from all sources and store them in a structured binary journal. Older-style text-based logging is handled by **rsyslog**, which writes to files under `/var/log/`.

**Think of it like this:** `journald` is a smart, indexed database of everything that happened on your system, while `/var/log/` files are the plain text printouts you can grep through.

### Exploring `/var/log`

Let's start by seeing what's in the central log directory:

```bash
ls -lh /var/log/
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/image.png)

You'll see a collection of files and folders. The exact contents vary by distribution and configuration, but here are common ones:

| File / Directory | What it contains | Availability |
|-----------------|-----------------|--------------|
| `syslog` | General system messages from most services | rsyslog-based systems |
| `auth.log` | Authentication events — logins, sudo usage, SSH attempts | Debian/Ubuntu with rsyslog |
| `kern.log` | Kernel-only log messages | Systems with rsyslog |
| `dpkg.log` | Package installation and removal history | Debian/Ubuntu systems |
| `apt/` | APT package manager logs | Debian/Ubuntu systems |
| `journal/` | The systemd binary journal data | systemd-based systems |
| `wtmp` | Login/logout history (binary format) | Most systems |
| `btmp` | Failed login attempts (binary format) | Most systems |
| `lastlog` | Last login time for each user (binary format) | Most systems |

**Note:** In minimal or containerized environments, many traditional log files may not exist. If you don't see `syslog`, `auth.log`, or `kern.log`, your system likely uses only the systemd journal or has limited logging configured.

**To check what log files are actually available on your system:**

```bash
sudo find /var/log -type f -name "*.log" 2>/dev/null
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/image-18.png)

## Part 2: Creating the Test Environment

Now let's set up our AppTrack scenario. We'll create the log directory, generate a realistic log file, and register a failing service so `journalctl` has something to show us.

### Step 1: Create the AppTrack Log Directory

```bash
sudo mkdir -p /var/log/apptrack
```

### Step 2: Generate the AppTrack Log File

This command creates a realistic log file that shows AppTrack starting up, running normally, developing memory issues, and finally crashing. Copy and run the entire block:

```bash
sudo tee /var/log/apptrack/apptrack.log > /dev/null << 'EOF'
2026-03-10 22:01:05 [INFO]  AppTrack v2.3.1 starting up
2026-03-10 22:01:05 [INFO]  Loading configuration from /etc/apptrack/config.yaml
2026-03-10 22:01:06 [INFO]  Database connection established (host=db-01, port=5432)
2026-03-10 22:01:06 [INFO]  Cache layer initialized (Redis 127.0.0.1:6379)
2026-03-10 22:01:07 [INFO]  HTTP server listening on 0.0.0.0:8080
2026-03-10 22:01:07 [INFO]  Worker pool started (workers=8)
2026-03-10 22:05:12 [INFO]  Processed 1200 requests (avg latency: 14ms)
2026-03-10 22:15:44 [INFO]  Processed 5800 requests (avg latency: 16ms)
2026-03-10 22:30:21 [INFO]  Processed 12400 requests (avg latency: 15ms)
2026-03-10 23:00:09 [INFO]  Processed 28900 requests (avg latency: 17ms)
2026-03-10 23:45:33 [WARN]  Memory usage at 72% (threshold: 80%)
2026-03-10 23:45:33 [WARN]  Request queue depth increasing (depth=312)
2026-03-10 23:51:07 [WARN]  Memory usage at 81% — exceeded soft threshold
2026-03-10 23:51:07 [WARN]  Slow query detected: SELECT * FROM events WHERE user_id=? (took 4821ms)
2026-03-10 23:51:45 [WARN]  Slow query detected: SELECT * FROM events WHERE user_id=? (took 5103ms)
2026-03-10 23:52:10 [WARN]  Request queue depth critical (depth=1847)
2026-03-10 23:52:33 [ERROR] Worker #3 timed out processing request (timeout=30s)
2026-03-10 23:52:45 [ERROR] Worker #7 timed out processing request (timeout=30s)
2026-03-10 23:53:01 [ERROR] Worker #1 timed out processing request (timeout=30s)
2026-03-10 23:53:14 [ERROR] Database connection pool exhausted (pool_size=20, waiting=48)
2026-03-10 23:53:14 [ERROR] Failed to acquire DB connection after 10s — dropping request
2026-03-10 23:53:15 [ERROR] Failed to acquire DB connection after 10s — dropping request
2026-03-10 23:53:20 [WARN]  Memory usage at 94% — approaching hard limit
2026-03-10 23:53:29 [ERROR] Cache write failure: Redis connection refused (ECONNREFUSED)
2026-03-10 23:53:29 [ERROR] Cache write failure: Redis connection refused (ECONNREFUSED)
2026-03-10 23:53:31 [CRITICAL] Memory usage at 99% — emergency shutdown initiated
2026-03-10 23:53:31 [CRITICAL] Flushing in-flight requests (in-flight=1204)
2026-03-10 23:53:32 [CRITICAL] Flush incomplete — 847 requests lost
2026-03-10 23:53:32 [CRITICAL] AppTrack terminated abnormally (exit code: 137)
EOF
```

Now verify the log was created:

```bash
wc -l /var/log/apptrack/apptrack.log
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/image-2.png)

You should see `29 /var/log/apptrack/apptrack.log`. We now have a 29-line log that tells the full story of AppTrack's last moments.

### Step 3: Write AppTrack Crash to the System Journal

Real services write to the systemd journal when they crash. Let's simulate that using `logger`, which lets you inject messages into the system log from the command line:

```bash
sudo logger -t apptrack -p daemon.err "AppTrack service crashed — exit code 137 (OOM kill)"
sudo logger -t apptrack -p daemon.warn "AppTrack: memory limit exceeded before shutdown"
sudo logger -t apptrack -p daemon.info "AppTrack: service restart scheduled in 30 seconds"
```

Breaking down the `logger` flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `-t apptrack` | Tag these messages as coming from "apptrack" |
| `-p daemon.err` | Set priority: facility `daemon`, level `err` |
| `-p daemon.warn` | Set priority: facility `daemon`, level `warn` |
| `-p daemon.info` | Set priority: facility `daemon`, level `info` |

**Why it matters**: `logger` is incredibly useful in shell scripts. When your backup script runs, you want it to write its status somewhere you can check later — `logger` is how you do that.

## Part 3: Reading the AppTrack Log File

Now let's put on our detective hat. The AppTrack log file is our primary evidence.

### Viewing the Full Log

```bash
cat /var/log/apptrack/apptrack.log
```

Reading the whole file gives us the complete picture, but in production, logs can be millions of lines. We need to be smarter.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/image-3.png)

### Viewing the End of the Log

The most recent entries — where the crash happened — are at the bottom. Use `tail` to jump straight there:

```bash
tail -15 /var/log/apptrack/apptrack.log
```

This shows us the last 15 lines — the critical window when everything fell apart.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/image-4.png)

### Real-Time Log Monitoring with `tail -f`

The `-f` flag (follow) keeps the file open and prints new lines as they're written. This is how you watch a live system:

```bash
tail -f /var/log/apptrack/apptrack.log
```

Now open a **second terminal** and append a new entry to simulate a live service writing a log:

```bash
echo "2026-03-11 02:47:13 [INFO]  AppTrack restarted — resuming normal operation" | sudo tee -a /var/log/apptrack/apptrack.log
```

The first terminal instantly shows the new line the moment it's written. This is the standard technique for watching any live log — nginx, postgres, your own application.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/image-5.png)

Press `Ctrl+C` to exit `tail -f`.

## Part 4: Filtering Logs with `grep`

Now let's find exactly what went wrong. `grep` is your most powerful tool for slicing through log files.

### Finding All Errors

```bash
grep "ERROR" /var/log/apptrack/apptrack.log
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/image-6.png)

This shows every line tagged `[ERROR]`. Already we can see the DB connection pool exhaustion and the Redis connection failures.

### Finding Critical Events Only

```bash
grep "CRITICAL" /var/log/apptrack/apptrack.log
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/image-7.png)

Four CRITICAL lines tell the exact story: memory hit 99%, emergency shutdown was initiated, the flush was incomplete, and the process died with exit code 137.

> **Note:** Exit code 137 means the process was killed by signal 9 (SIGKILL). On Linux, the OOM (Out of Memory) killer uses SIGKILL to terminate processes when the system runs out of RAM. This is a smoking gun.

### Showing Context Around a Match

Sometimes you want to see what happened just before and after an error. Use `-B` (before) and `-A` (after):

```bash
grep -B 3 -A 2 "CRITICAL" /var/log/apptrack/apptrack.log
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/image-8.png)

`-B 3` shows 3 lines before each CRITICAL match, `-A 2` shows 2 lines after. Now you can see the memory was already at 94% just 11 seconds before the crash.

### Finding the Timeline of Warnings

```bash
grep "WARN" /var/log/apptrack/apptrack.log
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/image-9.png)

The warnings give us the early warning signs: memory crossed 72% at 23:45, slow queries appeared at 23:51, and the request queue started backing up. There were 8 minutes of warning signs before the crash — plenty of time for an alert to have fired.

### Case-Insensitive Search

```bash
grep -i "memory" /var/log/apptrack/apptrack.log
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/image-10.png)

The `-i` flag makes the search case-insensitive, catching "Memory", "MEMORY", and "memory" all at once. This is useful when logs from different services use different capitalisation conventions.

### Counting Occurrences

How many errors were there total?

```bash
grep -c "ERROR" /var/log/apptrack/apptrack.log
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/image-11.png)

`-c` returns a count instead of the matching lines. Quick way to gauge the severity of an incident.

## Part 5: Investigating with `journalctl`

While the AppTrack log file is our application-specific record, `journalctl` gives us access to the **entire system journal** — including kernel messages, service lifecycle events, and everything else systemd captured.

### View the Full Journal (Recent Entries)

```bash
sudo journalctl -n 30
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/image-12.png)

`-n 30` shows the last 30 entries across the entire system. You'll see a mix of services and kernel messages — this is the bird's-eye view of what everyone on the system was doing at the time.

### Filter by Tag (Our AppTrack Messages)

Remember the messages we wrote with `logger -t apptrack`? Let's retrieve them:

```bash
sudo journalctl -t apptrack
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/image-13.png)

`-t` filters by the syslog identifier (tag). This pulls only the three messages we injected: the crash, the memory warning, and the restart notice.

### Filter by Time Window

An important distinction to understand: the timestamps inside `/var/log/apptrack/apptrack.log` are just **text we wrote into a file**. The systemd journal, however, records the real system time at which each event actually occurred. This means our `logger` messages were stamped with today's time — not the fictional 2026-03-10 dates in the log file.

To retrieve entries from around when you ran the `logger` commands, use a relative time:

```bash
sudo journalctl --since "5 minutes ago"
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/image-14.png)

Or narrow it to just the AppTrack tag in that window:

```bash
sudo journalctl -t apptrack --since "10 minutes ago"
```

`--since` and `--until` accept both relative expressions (`"1 hour ago"`, `"yesterday"`) and absolute timestamps (`"2026-03-11 14:00:00"`). In a real incident, you would use the absolute form to pin the exact window — but that only works when the journal entries themselves were recorded during that window.

### Common Time Shortcuts

```bash
# Everything since the system booted
sudo journalctl -b

# Last hour only
sudo journalctl --since "1 hour ago"

# Since yesterday
sudo journalctl --since yesterday
```

### Filter by Priority Level

Log messages have priority levels from 0 (emergency) to 7 (debug). To see only errors and above:

```bash
sudo journalctl -p err
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/image-15.png)

| Priority | Level | What it means |
|----------|-------|---------------|
| 0 | `emerg` | System is unusable |
| 1 | `alert` | Action must be taken immediately |
| 2 | `crit` | Critical conditions |
| 3 | `err` | Error conditions |
| 4 | `warning` | Warning conditions |
| 5 | `notice` | Normal but significant |
| 6 | `info` | Informational |
| 7 | `debug` | Debug-level messages |

`-p err` shows all messages at priority `err` and higher (err, crit, alert, emerg). In a post-incident review, this gives you the shortest list of things that were actually breaking.

### Follow the Journal in Real Time

Just like `tail -f`, `journalctl` can follow new entries live:

```bash
sudo journalctl -f
```

Open a second terminal and write another logger message to watch it appear instantly:

```bash
sudo logger -t apptrack -p daemon.info "AppTrack health check: OK (latency=12ms)"
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/image-16.png)

Press `Ctrl+C` to stop following.

### View Journal Disk Usage

The journal doesn't grow forever — it has size limits. Check how much space it's currently using:

```bash
sudo journalctl --disk-usage
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/image-17.png)

**Why it matters**: On a busy production server, the journal can consume significant disk space. Knowing its size helps you plan disk provisioning and set appropriate retention limits.

## Part 6: Log Rotation with `logrotate`

Imagine AppTrack runs for a year. Its log file would grow to gigabytes. The solution is **log rotation** — automatically archiving old logs and starting fresh ones on a schedule.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/Log-sequence.svg)

### Step 1: Install logrotate

`logrotate` is not pre-installed on all systems. Check first, then install if needed:

```bash
which logrotate
```

If the command returns nothing, install it:

```bash
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y logrotate
```

Verify the installation:

```bash
logrotate --version
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/image-19.png)

### Step 2: View the Default Configuration

```bash
sudo cat /etc/logrotate.conf
```

You should see output like this:

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/image-20.png)

Here is what each active setting does:

| Setting | Meaning |
|---------|---------|
| `weekly` | Rotate log files once a week |
| `su root adm` | Run logrotate as the `root` user with the `adm` group — matches the default ownership of `/var/log/` |
| `rotate 4` | Keep 4 archived copies before deleting the oldest (4 weeks of history) |
| `create` | After rotation, create a new empty log file in place of the old one |
| `#compress` | Compression is disabled globally — individual configs in `/etc/logrotate.d/` can override this |
| `include /etc/logrotate.d` | Load per-application rotation configs from this directory — this is where our AppTrack config will live |

### Step 3: Create a logrotate Config for AppTrack

```bash
sudo tee /etc/logrotate.d/apptrack > /dev/null << 'EOF'
/var/log/apptrack/apptrack.log {
    daily
    rotate 7
    compress
    delaycompress
    missingok
    notifempty
    create 0640 root adm
    postrotate
        # Signal apptrack to reopen its log file after rotation
        systemctl kill --kill-who=main --signal=USR1 apptrack.service 2>/dev/null || true
    endscript
}
EOF
```

This tells logrotate to:
- Rotate the AppTrack log **daily**
- Keep **7 days** of history
- **Compress** archived copies
- Create the new log with permissions **0640** owned by **root:adm**
- After rotation, send a **USR1 signal** to AppTrack so it reopens its log file handle

### Verify the Configuration

```bash
sudo logrotate --debug /etc/logrotate.d/apptrack
```

You should see output like this:

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/image-21.png)

Here is what each part of this output tells you:

| Output line | What it means |
|-------------|---------------|
| `warning: logrotate in debug mode does nothing` | Confirms this is a dry run — no files are touched |
| `reading config file /etc/logrotate.d/apptrack` | Config was found and loaded successfully |
| `state file does not exist` | First time running — logrotate has no rotation history yet |
| `rotating pattern: after 1 days (7 rotations)` | Confirms your `daily` and `rotate 7` settings were read correctly |
| `log does not need rotating` | The log was already rotated within the last 24 hours — nothing to do |

> **Note:** The "log does not need rotating" message is expected. Since we just created the log file, logrotate sees it as recently rotated and skips it. To force a rotation regardless, use `--force` in the next step.

### Trigger a Manual Rotation

```bash
sudo logrotate --force /etc/logrotate.d/apptrack
```

Now check the log directory:

```bash
ls -lh /var/log/apptrack/
```

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/image-22.png)

You should see:
- `apptrack.log` — a new, empty log file (fresh start)
- `apptrack.log.1` — the rotated archive (or `apptrack.log.1.gz` if compression ran)

**Why it matters**: Without log rotation, a busy server will eventually fill its disk with old log files, causing services to crash. Log rotation is a critical piece of any production system — and neglecting it is a very common cause of late-night production incidents.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/1bc572d6354bd0f165f066ab72b933a5a47457f7/Linux%20Labs/Lab%2009/images/life-log.svg)

## Conclusion

In this lab, we took a hands-on journey through the Linux logging stack. We started with an unexplained outage, generated a realistic log file to simulate the incident, and then used the full toolkit of Linux logging tools to reconstruct exactly what happened. The commands you practiced here — `journalctl`, `tail -f`, `grep`, `logger`, and `logrotate` — are the first tools any Linux engineer reaches for when something goes wrong.
